stem: How does reduced sleep affect risk-taking behaviour in adolescents?

options.text: Reduced sleep impairs prefrontal cortex function and self-regulation
Reduced sleep improves motor coordination and encourages physical risk-taking
Risk-taking is only linked to excessive sleep, not sleep restriction
There is no established link between sleep and brain function in adolescents
Reduced sleep mainly increases growth hormone secretion and reduces impulsivity

explanation: Reduced sleep impairs prefrontal cortex function and self-regulation, which increases impulsive and risky behaviour in adolescents.

optionExplanations.A: Correct because reduced sleep disrupts prefrontal cortex function, weakening impulse control and self-regulation.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because sleep deprivation impairs, rather than improves, coordination and judgement.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because reduced sleep is associated with increased, not absent, risk-taking behaviour.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because sleep and prefrontal cortex function are clearly linked in adolescent behaviour and self-regulation.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because the main effect relevant to risk-taking is impaired prefrontal control, not increased growth hormone secretion.

source.hint: Identify which part of the brain is responsible for impulse control.
